INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Inflamm:
Overview — The Inflammatory Response
Inflammation is the body's protective response to injury or infection — bringing immune cells and mediators to the site to destroy the cause, clear debris, and begin repair.
The organising principle: acute inflammation has a vascular response (↑blood flow + ↑permeability) and a cellular response (recruiting neutrophils to the site), driven by chemical mediators — producing the cardinal signs. It either resolves or, if unresolved, becomes chronic. It's protective, but excessive/chronic inflammation causes disease.
Why it matters: underpins the cardinal signs, wound healing, sepsis (SIRS), the acute-phase response (CRP), chronic inflammatory disease, and how NSAIDs/steroids work — cross-ref innate immunity (inflammation is part of it), pain physiology (mediators), sepsis, the acute-phase response, NSAIDs/steroids.
The Cardinal Signs — what inflammation looks like
The five classic signs (derivable from the vascular + cellular changes below):
Sign Cause
Redness (rubor)↑blood flow (vasodilation)
Heat (calor)↑blood flow
Swelling (tumor)↑vascular permeability → fluid leaks into tissue (exudate)
Pain (dolor)Mediators (bradykinin, prostaglandins) sensitise nerves (cross-ref pain)
Loss of functionPain + swelling
The point: all five fall out of the two core processes — vasodilation (redness/heat) + increased permeability (swelling) + mediators (pain).
The Vascular Response — the first phase (high-yield)
The blood vessels at the injury site change to deliver immune cells + mediators:
Change Effect
Vasodilation↑blood flow to the area → redness + heat (mediated by histamine, prostaglandins, NO)
↑Vascular permeabilityEndothelial cells contract → gaps form → fluid + proteins leak out (exudate) → swelling
StasisSlowed flow (from fluid loss + haemoconcentration) → lets leucocytes marginate
The exudate point: the fluid that leaks out is protein-rich (exudate) — carrying antibodies, complement, and fibrinogen (which forms fibrin to wall off the area) → distinguishes inflammatory exudate from a simple transudate.
The Cellular Response — recruiting the cells (high-yield)
Neutrophils are the first cells recruited to the site, in a defined sequence:
Step What happens
MarginationSlowed flow (stasis) → neutrophils move to the vessel edge
Rolling + adhesionNeutrophils bind the endothelium (via selectins → integrins)
Diapedesis (transmigration)Neutrophils squeeze through the vessel wall into the tissue
ChemotaxisNeutrophils migrate toward the pathogen (following chemical gradients — chemokines, complement C5a)
PhagocytosisNeutrophils engulf + destroy the pathogen (aided by opsonisation — antibody/complement coating)
The neutrophil-first point (high-yield): neutrophils arrive first (acute inflammation), then macrophages later (clean-up + chronic); this is why the FBC shows neutrophilia in acute bacterial infection (cross-ref white cells).
Opsonisation: coating the pathogen with antibody/complement → makes phagocytosis far more efficient ("opsonins" = "to prepare for eating").
The Chemical Mediators — the drivers (high-yield, the drug targets)
Inflammation is coordinated by chemical mediators:
Mediator Source Action
HistamineMast cellsVasodilation + ↑permeability (early) — antihistamines block it
ProstaglandinsFrom arachidonic acid (COX)Vasodilation, pain, fever — NSAIDs block COX
LeukotrienesFrom arachidonic acid (lipoxygenase)Bronchoconstriction, ↑permeability — leukotriene antagonists (asthma)
Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6)MacrophagesThe systemic response — fever, acute-phase proteins; TNF/IL-6 = biologic drug targets
BradykininPlasmaPain + vasodilation
Complement (C3a, C5a)PlasmaChemotaxis + mast cell activation (cross-ref complement)
The drug-target payoffs (high-yield):
  • NSAIDs block COX → ↓prostaglandins → anti-inflammatory + analgesic + antipyretic (cross-ref pain)
  • Steroids broadly suppress inflammation (↓ mediators, ↓ phospholipase → ↓ arachidonic acid pathway) — the most powerful anti-inflammatories
  • Biologics (anti-TNF, anti-IL-6) block specific cytokines (rheumatoid arthritis, IBD)
The Systemic Response — inflammation beyond the local site (high-yield)
Cytokines (TNF-α, IL-1, IL-6) released into the blood produce systemic effects:
Effect Mechanism
FeverCytokines → hypothalamus → ↑temperature set point (cross-ref homeostasis)
Acute-phase proteinsLiver produces CRP, fibrinogen, ferritin (IL-6-driven) → CRP is the clinical inflammatory marker
Leucocytosis↑white cell production (neutrophilia in bacterial infection)
Malaise/anorexiaCytokine effects
The CRP/ESR point (high-yield): CRP (rises fast, IL-6-driven) and ESR (slower, fibrinogen-related) are the clinical markers of inflammation → used to detect + monitor inflammatory/infective disease.
SIRS/sepsis (the extreme): an overwhelming systemic inflammatory response → SIRS → sepsis (dysregulated response to infection → organ dysfunction) — cross-ref sepsis.
Acute vs Chronic Inflammation & Outcomes — the resolution question (high-yield)
Acute inflammation (rapid, neutrophil-driven, short-lived) can have several outcomes:
Outcome What happens
ResolutionThe cause is cleared → tissue returns to normal (the ideal)
Chronic inflammationIf unresolved → shifts to macrophages + lymphocytes → ongoing tissue damage + repair
Fibrosis/scarringRepair with fibrous tissue (if tissue can't regenerate)
AbscessLocalised collection of pus (dead neutrophils + debris)
Chronic inflammation (high-yield): macrophage + lymphocyte-driven (not neutrophils), with simultaneous tissue destruction + repair (fibrosis) → underlies TB, rheumatoid arthritis, IBD, atherosclerosis, chronic infection → often with granuloma formation (organised macrophages — TB, sarcoid, Crohn's).
The acute-vs-chronic cell distinction: acute = neutrophils; chronic = macrophages + lymphocytes.

NSAIDsBlock COX → ↓prostaglandins (anti-inflammatory/analgesic/antipyretic)
SteroidsBroad anti-inflammatory (↓mediators)

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Transpl:
Overview — Transplant Immunology & Rejection
The immunology of why grafts get rejected and how we prevent it — the generic mechanisms underlying organ transplantation (kidney, liver, heart, lung, marrow).
The central problem: the recipient's immune system recognises donor tissue as non-self (via HLA mismatch) → mounts a rejection response → graft damage.
The spine: HLA matching → the three rejection types (by timing + mechanism) → immunosuppression to prevent them. Cross-ref: renal transplant (kidney-specific timeline/regimen lives there), immunity/immunodeficiency (MHC, T-cells), hypersensitivity (rejection maps onto Gell & Coombs).
The Immunological Basis — HLA & Matching
  • HLA (human leukocyte antigen) = the human MHC — cell-surface molecules distinguishing self from non-self; the more mismatched, the stronger the rejection
  • MHC Class I (HLA-A, -B, -C) — all nucleated cells, recognised by CD8+ T-cells; MHC Class II (HLA-DR, -DQ, -DP) — APCs/B-cells, recognised by CD4+ T-cells
  • Most important to match: HLA-A, -B, and -DR (the "6-antigen match"); DR is the most significant
  • ABO blood group must also be compatible (ABO incompatibility → hyperacute rejection)
Pre-transplant crossmatch: recipient serum tested against donor lymphocytes to detect pre-formed anti-HLA antibodies — a positive crossmatch → hyperacute rejection → contraindication.
Allorecognition — how the immune system "sees" the graft
Direct pathway
Recipient T-cells recognise intact donor HLA on donor APCs → drives acute rejection (early, vigorous).
Indirect pathway
Recipient APCs process donor HLA and present it → drives chronic rejection (later).
The key: T-cell recognition of donor HLA is the engine of rejection.
Types of Rejection — timing names the mechanism
Rejection Timing Mechanism HS type Outcome
HyperacuteMins–hoursPre-formed recipient antibodies vs donor ABO/HLA → complement → thrombosis + necrosisIIIrreversible → remove graft; prevented by crossmatch
AcuteDays–6 monthsT-cell-mediated (cellular) ± antibody; HLA mismatchIVOften reversible with ↑immunosuppression
ChronicMonths–yearsAntibody + cell-mediated → fibrosis, vascular damage (graft vasculopathy)MixedLargely irreversible → graft failure
Memory hook: hyperacute = preformed antibodies (Type II, prevented by crossmatch); acute = T-cells/HLA mismatch (Type IV, treatable); chronic = fibrosis (untreatable).
Graft-versus-Host Disease (GVHD) — the reverse
The opposite of rejection: in bone marrow/stem cell transplants, the donor's immune cells attack the recipient's tissues (graft attacks host, not host attacks graft).
  • Targets (classic triad): skin (rash), gut (diarrhoea), liver (deranged LFTs/jaundice)
  • Acute (<100 days) vs chronic; managed with immunosuppression; prevented by HLA matching + T-cell depletion
The key contrast: solid-organ transplant → host rejects graft; marrow transplant → graft rejects host (GVHD).
Immunosuppression — preventing rejection
The strategy: induction (intense, peri-transplant) then maintenance (lifelong, lower-dose); usually triple therapy.
Class Examples Mechanism
Calcineurin inhibitorsTacrolimus, ciclosporinBlock calcineurin → ↓IL-2 → ↓T-cell activation (backbone; nephrotoxic, narrow TI → TDM)
AntiproliferativesMycophenolate, azathioprineInhibit purine synthesis → ↓lymphocyte proliferation
CorticosteroidsPrednisoloneBroad anti-inflammatory/immunosuppressive
mTOR inhibitorsSirolimusBlock T-cell proliferation
Biologics (induction)Basiliximab (anti-IL-2R), ATGDeplete/block T-cells
Standard maintenance: tacrolimus + mycophenolate + prednisolone. Treating acute rejection: high-dose steroids first-line ± antibody therapy.
Complications of Immunosuppression — the lifelong trade-off
Infection — the big one
Opportunistic: CMV, PCP (prophylaxis: co-trimoxazole), fungal, BK virus, reactivation of TB/hepatitis. These patients have iatrogenic T-cell deficiency (cross-ref immunodeficiency).
Malignancy
Skin cancers (esp. SCC — regular skin surveillance), post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease (PTLD — EBV-driven), others.
  • Drug-specific: calcineurin inhibitor nephrotoxicity, new-onset diabetes, hypertension, tremor (tacrolimus); marrow suppression (azathioprine — check TPMT first); gum hypertrophy/hirsutism (ciclosporin)
  • Cardiovascular risk, osteoporosis (steroids)

Overview — Infection Control / HCAIs
Two linked ideas: HCAIs (healthcare-associated/nosocomial infections — acquired ≥48h after admission, not incubating on arrival) and infection control (the measures that prevent them).
The organising principle = the chain of infection: every infection follows a predictable chain, and breaking any single link prevents transmission. The single most effective intervention = hand hygiene.
Cross-ref: antimicrobial stewardship (antibiotic overuse → C. diff/MRSA), notifiable diseases, sepsis, C. diff/infective diarrhoea, the specific HCAIs (HAP, CLABSI, CAUTI, SSI).
The Chain of Infection — six links to break
Link What it is How to break it
1. Infectious agentThe pathogenAntimicrobials, sterilisation
2. ReservoirWhere it lives (people, equipment, water)Cleaning, decontamination
3. Portal of exitHow it leaves (secretions, blood, faeces)Respiratory hygiene, cover wounds
4. Mode of transmissionContact / droplet / airborne / vehicleHand hygiene, PPE, isolation
5. Portal of entryHow it enters (wounds, lines, mucosa)Aseptic technique, catheter care
6. Susceptible hostThe patient at riskVaccination, treating comorbidity, nutrition
Transmission routes (determine the precautions): contact (direct/indirect — MRSA, C. diff), droplet (large particles, settle quickly — influenza, COVID, pertussis, meningococcus), airborne (small particles, stay suspended — TB, measles, varicella), vehicle/vector (food, water, blood).
Standard Precautions — EVERY patient, always
The baseline applied to all patient care (assume any patient may be infectious):
  • Hand hygiene (the foundation)
  • PPE (gloves, apron/gown, mask, eye protection — as risk dictates)
  • Sharps safety (no re-sheathing; sharps bins)
  • Respiratory hygiene ("catch it, bin it, kill it")
  • Safe waste + linen disposal
  • Cleaning + decontamination of equipment/environment
  • Aseptic technique for invasive procedures
Hand Hygiene — the single most important measure

MRSA & C. diff in Focus
MRSA
Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams (altered PBP2a); screen on admission (nasal/groin swab) → decolonise (mupirocin + chlorhexidine); contact precautions; treat infection with vancomycin/teicoplanin/linezolid (cross-ref antibiotics).
C. difficile
Antibiotic use → loss of gut flora → toxin-producing C. diff overgrowth → pseudomembranous colitis. The "4 Cs" high-risk antibiotics: clindamycin, cephalosporins, co-amoxiclav, ciprofloxacin. Isolate + soap-and-water + oral vancomycin/fidaxomicin (not metronidazole first-line now); stop the offending antibiotic.

  • Care bundles (CLABSI, CAUTI, ventilator bundles)
  • Surveillance + audit (mandatory MRSA bacteraemia + C. diff reporting)
  • Antimicrobial stewardship (cross-ref), environmental cleaning
  • Isolation facilities (side rooms, negative pressure)
  • Staff vaccination (flu, hepatitis B), education + hand-hygiene audits
  • Outbreak management (identify, isolate, cohort, deep clean, involve IPC team)
  • Aseptic Non-Touch Technique (ANTT) for invasive procedures

What Microbiology Is & Why It Matters

Microbiology = the study of microorganisms — organisms too small to see with the naked eye — and their interaction with the host. Clinically it underpins diagnosis (what's the bug?), treatment (what kills it?) and prevention (infection control + vaccines).

The core organising idea — three sequential questions: (1) WHAT is the organism? (classification/identification), (2) is it CAUSING disease? (commensal vs pathogen; colonisation vs infection), and (3) how do I TREAT + PREVENT it? (antimicrobials, infection control). This tab builds the framework for question 1 + the concepts behind question 2; the organism tabs handle the rest.
The Classification Tree — The Major Groups

Microbes divide first by cellular organisation, then into the clinically important groups:

GroupCell typeKey featuresGenome
Bacteriaprokaryote (no nucleus)peptidoglycan wall, binary fission, free-livingDNA (circular)
Virusesacellularobligate intracellular; protein capsid ± envelope; hijack host machineryDNA or RNA
Fungieukaryotechitin wall; yeasts (single-celled) or moulds (hyphae)DNA
Parasiteseukaryoteprotozoa (single-celled) or helminths (worms)DNA
Prionsnot an organismmisfolded protein — NO nucleic acidnone
The prokaryote vs eukaryote divide: bacteria are PROKARYOTES (no nucleus, no organelles, 70S ribosomes); fungi + parasites are EUKARYOTES (nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes) — this difference is exactly what antimicrobials exploit (antibiotics target the bacterial 70S ribosome/peptidoglycan wall, which human cells lack → selective toxicity).
The rule: bacteria (prokaryote) · viruses (acellular, DNA or RNA) · fungi (eukaryote, chitin wall) · parasites (eukaryote — protozoa/helminths) · prions (protein, no nucleic acid) — the six-fold framework.
Size Scale
A rough size hierarchy (helps understand filtration, microscopy + behaviour): prions < viruses (nm) < bacteria (~1–10 µm) < fungi/protozoa < helminths (mm–cm, visible).
The rule: viruses are much smaller than bacteria (need electron microscopy / pass through filters that trap bacteria); helminths are macroscopic.
Commensal vs Pathogen; Colonisation vs Infection

The normal flora (microbiota): we are colonised by vast numbers of commensal microbes (skin, gut, mouth, vagina) that are normally harmless or beneficial (compete with pathogens, aid digestion, prime immunity).

TermMeaning
Commensallives on/in us without causing harm (normal flora)
Pathogenan organism capable of causing disease
Colonisationpresent + multiplying, but NOT causing disease/host response
Infectioncausing tissue damage + a host response (disease)
Opportunistic pathogena commensal/low-virulence organism that causes disease only when defences are down
Context-dependence: the SAME organism can be a harmless commensal in one site + a dangerous pathogen in another — E. coli (gut commensal) causes disease in the urinary tract/bloodstream; Staph aureus (nasal commensal) causes disease in a wound or on a heart valve. Where the organism is matters as much as what it is.
The clinical implication: a positive culture does NOT always mean infection — it may be colonisation or contamination → interpret in context (host response? symptoms? inflammatory markers?). Commensal ≠ pathogen; colonisation ≠ infection; an opportunist causes disease only when defences fail.
Virulence — How Microbes Cause Disease

Virulence = the degree of pathogenicity — how effectively an organism causes disease, determined by virulence factors:

Capsuleresists phagocytosis (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis)

Enzymesspread / tissue damage (coagulase, hyaluronidase)

Biofilmsprotect organisms on prostheses/catheters → chronic, resistant infection
ExotoxinEndotoxin

Natureproteinlipopolysaccharide

The rule: virulence factors = adhesins, capsule, toxins (exotoxin protein vs endotoxin/LPS), enzymes, immune evasion, biofilms; endotoxin (Gram-negative LPS) drives sepsis.
The Chain of Infection & Transmission
Infection requires a chain: pathogen → reservoir → portal of exit → mode of transmission → portal of entry → susceptible host. Breaking any link prevents infection (the basis of infection control).
Modes of transmission: contact (direct/indirect), droplet, airborne, faecal-oral, vector-borne, vertical (mother→child), and blood-borne.
The rule: infection control works by breaking the chain (hand hygiene breaks contact spread; isolation breaks droplet/airborne).
Koch's Postulates
Koch's postulates — the classic criteria for proving an organism causes a disease: the organism is found in all cases, isolated + grown in pure culture, reproduces the disease when introduced into a healthy host, and is re-isolated from that host.
The caveat: they don't hold for all pathogens (uncultureable organisms, asymptomatic carriers, viruses) — but remain the conceptual foundation of causation in microbiology.

What Bacteria Are & Why the Framework Matters

Bacteria = single-celled PROKARYOTES — no nucleus, no organelles, a circular DNA chromosome, 70S ribosomes, and (usually) a peptidoglycan cell wall — reproducing by binary fission.

The core idea — classify along a few axes and let position predict behaviour: (1) the GRAM STAIN (the single most important lab step — cell-wall structure), (2) SHAPE (cocci vs bacilli), (3) ARRANGEMENT (clusters/chains/pairs), and (4) OXYGEN requirement. A few vital organisms don't fit the Gram stain (atypicals, mycobacteria, spirochaetes). Place an organism on this grid and you can predict its Gram appearance, likely antibiotic susceptibility + typical disease.

Steps: crystal violet → iodine (mordant) → alcohol (decolouriser) → safranin (counterstain).
The rule: Gram-positive = PURPLE, thick peptidoglycan, no endotoxin; Gram-negative = PINK, thin peptidoglycan + outer membrane + LPS/endotoxin (→ Gram-negative sepsis). The single most useful bacterial fact.

What Viruses Are & Why They're Different

Viruses = acellular, obligate intracellular parasites — a nucleic-acid genome (DNA OR RNA) inside a protein CAPSID, sometimes wrapped in a lipid ENVELOPE. They have no metabolic machinery of their own → they must hijack a host cell's ribosomes + enzymes to replicate.

The core idea — a virus is not a cell: no cell wall, no ribosomes, no metabolism to poison → the antibacterial drugs that exploit those targets are useless, and antivirals must target the few virus-specific steps (entry, genome replication, protein processing, release). Master axes: (1) genome — DNA vs RNA (the key divide), (2) envelope (enveloped vs non-enveloped), (3) replication strategy (esp. retroviruses + hepadnaviruses).
Viruses cause a huge share of infection (respiratory, GI, hepatitis, HIV, herpesviruses, oncogenic viruses) — and are why “it's probably viral → supportive care, no antibiotics” is such a common conclusion.

What Fungi Are & Why They Matter

Fungi = EUKARYOTES (nucleus, organelles, 80S ribosomes) with a cell wall of CHITIN + β-glucans and a membrane containing ERGOSTEROL (not cholesterol). They exist as yeasts, moulds, or dimorphic forms.

The core idea — two features drive everything: (1) fungi are EUKARYOTES → they share much of our cell machinery → selective toxicity is HARD (antifungals exploit the few fungus-specific structures — ergosterol + chitin/glucan, both absent from human cells). (2) Most fungal disease is OPPORTUNISTIC — serious infection when defences are down (immunocompromise, neutropenia, HIV, broad-spectrum antibiotics, lines, diabetes).
Severity tracks the host's immune state — from trivial (athlete's foot, thrush) to life-threatening (invasive aspergillosis, cryptococcal meningitis, PCP).

What Prions Are & Why They're the Outlier

Prions = infectious PROTEINS — uniquely, they contain NO nucleic acid (no DNA or RNA). A prion is a misfolded form of a normal host protein (PrP) that propagates by converting normal, correctly-folded protein into the abnormal form — a self-templating chain reaction.

The core idea — prions break every rule: no genome, no cell, no replication machinery — just a rogue protein shape that corrupts its normal counterpart. This explains everything: (1) they cause neurodegeneration (misfolded PrP → spongiform change → progressive, fatal dementia); (2) they trigger no immune/inflammatory response (the body sees “self” → no fever, no antibodies, normal CSF); (3) they are extraordinarily resistant to sterilisation (no nucleic acid to damage).
The clinical signature: a rapidly progressive dementia + neurological decline that is uniformly FATAL, with no inflammation and no cure. A classic infection-control + neurology crossover.

Resultaggregates → accumulate in neurons → SPONGIFORM (vacuolated) change → neurodegeneration
Key point: prions replicate by CONFORMATIONAL conversion (changing the SHAPE of an existing protein), NOT by copying a genetic code — the “information” is in the misfolded shape itself.
The resistance point: no nucleic acid to destroy → prions resist standard sterilisation (heat/autoclaving, formaldehyde, alcohol, radiation) → need special decontamination (extended high-temperature autoclaving, sodium hydroxide/hypochlorite) or single-use instruments for neurosurgical/ophthalmic/tonsillar procedures.

Overview — Membrane Transport & the Resting Membrane Potential
The cell membrane is a selective barrier — it controls what enters and leaves the cell, and this control creates the ion gradients that underlie the resting membrane potential (the electrical charge across the membrane) essential for all excitable tissue.
The organising principle: the membrane is selectively permeable, using different transport mechanisms for different substances; the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase sets up ion gradients that (with the membrane's K⁺ permeability) create the resting membrane potential — the foundation for nerve, muscle, and cardiac action potentials.
Why it matters: the foundation beneath every action potential (nerve, muscle, cardiac), the effect of electrolytes on excitable tissue, and how drugs/nutrients cross membranes — cross-ref the neuron/AP, cardiac AP, tubular reabsorption (Na⁺-driven transport), the electrolyte effects, cell signalling (next subtab).
The Cell Membrane — the structure
  • A phospholipid bilayer (hydrophilic heads out, hydrophobic tails in) with embedded proteins (channels, transporters, receptors)
The permeability principle: the lipid bilayer lets small, lipid-soluble (non-polar) molecules cross freely (O₂, CO₂, steroids, lipid-soluble drugs), but blocks large or charged/polar molecules (ions, glucose) → these need transport proteins.
The consequence: this selective permeability is what allows the cell to maintain a different internal environment from the outside (including the ion gradients for the membrane potential).
The Transport Mechanisms — passive vs active
Mechanism Energy? Direction Examples
Simple diffusionPassive (no ATP)Down the gradientO₂, CO₂, lipid-soluble molecules (cross the bilayer directly)
Facilitated diffusionPassiveDown the gradientGlucose (GLUT), ions through channels — via a protein
OsmosisPassiveWater down its osmotic gradientWater (via aquaporins)
Primary active transportActive (uses ATP directly)Against the gradientNa⁺/K⁺ ATPase, Ca²⁺ ATPase, proton pump
Secondary active transportActive (uses an ion gradient, not ATP directly)Against the gradientGlucose-Na⁺ cotransport (SGLT), Na⁺/H⁺ exchange
The passive-vs-active distinction: passive = down the gradient, no energy (diffusion, facilitated diffusion, osmosis); active = against the gradient, needs energy (directly as ATP, or borrowed from an ion gradient).
Secondary active transport (high-yield): doesn't use ATP directly — it uses the energy stored in an ion gradient (usually the Na⁺ gradient made by the Na⁺/K⁺ pump) to move something else against its gradient → e.g. SGLT (glucose rides in on the Na⁺ gradient — cross-ref renal tubular reabsorption, gut glucose absorption).
The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase — the master pump (core)
  • The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase is the key active transporter, found in every cell:
    • Pumps 3 Na⁺ OUT and 2 K⁺ IN per ATP (against their gradients)
    • → maintains high Na⁺ outside, high K⁺ inside (the fundamental cellular ion gradients)
Why it matters (the payoffs):
  • It sets up the gradients for the resting membrane potential and all action potentials
  • It powers secondary active transport (the Na⁺ gradient it creates drives glucose/amino acid uptake — cross-ref renal/gut)
  • It's electrogenic (3 out, 2 in → net loss of positive charge → contributes slightly to the negative resting potential)
The clinical link: digoxin inhibits the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase in cardiac muscle → ↑intracellular Na⁺ → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (via Na⁺/Ca²⁺ exchange) → ↑contractility (positive inotrope).
The Resting Membrane Potential — the core concept (high-yield)
At rest, the inside of the cell is negative relative to the outside (~−70 mV in neurons, ~−90 mV in cardiac/skeletal muscle) — created by:
Factor Contribution
Na⁺/K⁺ ATPaseSets up the ion gradients (high K⁺ in, high Na⁺ out)
K⁺ leak channelsThe membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest → K⁺ leaks out down its gradient → leaves the inside negative
Large intracellular anionsProteins/phosphates (negative, can't leave) add to the negativity
The key concept: the resting potential is set mainly by potassium — because the membrane is most permeable to K⁺ at rest, the resting potential sits close to the K⁺ equilibrium potential (~−90 mV). K⁺ leaking out is what makes the inside negative.
The equilibrium potential idea (brief): each ion has an equilibrium potential (the voltage at which its electrical + chemical gradients balance) — the Nernst equation gives it; the resting potential is a weighted average dominated by the most permeable ion (K⁺) (concept-level, no need to calculate).
Why This Matters for Excitable Tissue — the payoff
  • The resting potential is the starting point for every action potential: a stimulus depolarises the membrane toward threshold → voltage-gated Na⁺ channels open → the AP fires (cross-ref neuron/AP, cardiac AP)
The electrolyte link (high-yield): because the resting potential depends on the K⁺ gradient, changing extracellular K⁺ shifts it:
  • Hyperkalaemia (↑extracellular K⁺) → ↓the K⁺ gradient → depolarises the resting potential → initially more excitable, then (sustained) inactivates Na⁺ channels → inexcitable → cardiac arrest (the ECG changes + the danger of hyperkalaemia — cross-ref)
  • Hypokalaemia → hyperpolarises → arrhythmia risk
The point: this is why potassium disorders are cardiac emergencies — they directly alter the resting membrane potential of excitable tissue (cross-ref cardiac AP, electrolytes).

Overview — Cell Signalling
Cells communicate via chemical signals (hormones, neurotransmitters, local mediators) that bind receptors and trigger a response — the basis of coordinated body function.
The organising principle: signalling depends on where the receptor is, which is determined by whether the signal molecule is water-soluble (can't cross the membrane → surface receptors) or lipid-soluble (crosses the membrane → intracellular receptors). The receptor type then determines the speed and mechanism of the response.
Why it matters: underpins hormone action (fast peptide vs slow steroid), receptor pharmacology (agonists/antagonists), the second-messenger systems, and why some hormones act in seconds and others over hours — cross-ref the hypothalamic-pituitary axes + all endocrine notes (hormone action), the autonomic NS (receptors), membrane transport, drug pharmacology.

The point: the same principle (signal → receptor → response) operates whether the signal travels body-wide (endocrine) or just across a synapse (neuronal) — differing mainly in distance + speed.

The key concept (the whole framework): water-soluble → surface receptor → second messenger → fast, short; lipid-soluble → intracellular receptor → gene transcription → slow, long → this single divide explains why adrenaline acts in seconds but cortisol/thyroid hormone take hours.
The transport corollary: lipid-soluble hormones (steroids, thyroid) are carried bound to plasma proteins in the blood (they're not water-soluble) → only the free fraction is active (cross-ref thyroid — free T4).

  • IP₃ + DAG → ↑intracellular Ca²⁺ (another major pathway)
  • Ca²⁺ itself (a key intracellular signal — cross-ref muscle contraction)
The amplification point (high-yield): one hormone molecule → activates many G-proteins → each makes many cAMP → each activates many enzymes → a cascade that massively amplifies a tiny signal (why hormones work at nanomolar concentrations).
Intracellular Receptors & Gene Transcription — the slow pathway
  • Lipid-soluble signals (steroids, thyroid hormone, vitamin D) cross the membrane and bind intracellular receptors (cytoplasm/nucleus):
    • The hormone-receptor complex acts as a transcription factor → binds DNA → alters gene expression → new protein synthesis
The consequences: this is slow (hours-days — takes time to make new proteins) but produces lasting effects → why steroid effects (cortisol, aldosterone) build up over hours and persist.
The steroid pharmacology link: this is why therapeutic steroids take time to work + why they have widespread effects (altering transcription across many tissues) — cross-ref steroids.

Overview — Body Fluid Compartments & Osmosis
Body water is distributed between compartments (inside vs outside cells, and within the extracellular space), and water moves between them by osmosis — driven by solute concentrations.
The organising principle: total body water splits into intracellular and extracellular compartments, kept separate by cell membranes; water moves freely between them by osmosis (following solutes), while the solutes that can't cross determine where water goes. Sodium is the main extracellular solute (so it governs extracellular volume), and osmosis explains fluid shifts, oedema, and IV fluid behaviour.
Why it matters: underpins IV fluid therapy, oedema, dehydration, hypo/hypernatraemia, and cellular swelling/shrinking — cross-ref ADH/water balance + renal sodium handling (the regulation), capillary Starling forces (oedema), membrane transport, hyponatraemia, fluid resuscitation.

Total body water ≈ 60% of body weight, split by the "60-40-20 rule":

Total body water~60%100%
Intracellular fluid (ICF)~40%~⅔ (the majority — inside cells)
Extracellular fluid (ECF)~20%~⅓
— Interstitial (between cells)~15%~¾ of ECF
— Plasma (intravascular)~5%~¼ of ECF
The key split: ⅔ intracellular, ⅓ extracellular (and of the ECF, ¾ interstitial + ¼ plasma) — the "60-40-20" rule.
The barriers: the cell membrane separates ICF from ECF (water crosses freely, solutes selectively — cross-ref membrane transport); the capillary wall separates plasma from interstitium (water + small solutes cross, proteins mostly don't — cross-ref Starling forces).

The sodium point (high-yield): because sodium is the main extracellular solute, total body sodium determines ECF volume → this is why sodium = volume (cross-ref renal sodium handling + ADH note). Add sodium → hold water in the ECF → ↑volume; lose sodium → lose ECF volume.
The corollary: water balance (osmolality) is controlled by ADH; sodium (volume) by aldosterone/RAAS → the distinction from your ADH note.
Osmosis & Tonicity — the water-movement mechanism (high-yield)
  • Osmosis = water moves across a semipermeable membrane from low solute (high water) → high solute (low water) concentration → water follows solute
  • Osmolality = the concentration of osmotically active particles (mainly Na⁺, glucose, urea in the ECF); normal ~285–295 mOsm/kg

HypertonicWater moves out of cells → cells shrink — e.g. hypernatraemia
The key clinical concept: changes in ECF osmolality shift water in or out of cells → hyponatraemia (low ECF osmolality) → water moves into cells → cellular swelling (dangerous in the brain → cerebral oedema); hypernatraemia → cells shrink.
The effective-osmole point: urea crosses membranes freely so it's an ineffective osmole (doesn't shift water); Na⁺ and glucose are effective osmoles (they do shift water — why hyperglycaemia causes hyponatraemia by pulling water out of cells).

Overview — Homeostatic Principles
Homeostasis = the maintenance of a stable internal environment despite external changes — the fundamental organising principle of all physiology.
The organising principle: the body keeps regulated variables (temperature, pH, glucose, ions, blood pressure, osmolality) within narrow ranges using negative feedback control systems — a sensor, control centre, and effector. Understanding this framework makes every regulatory system (endocrine axes, BP control, acid-base, glucose) an instance of the same logic, and disease is often a failure of homeostasis.
Why it matters: the unifying framework beneath every regulatory system you've built (hormonal axes, BP regulation, acid-base, glucose, fluid balance, temperature) — cross-ref the hypothalamic-pituitary axes, BP regulation, acid-base, glucose homeostasis, ADH/fluid balance (all instances of this).
What Homeostasis Regulates — the "set points"
The body tightly regulates the variables its cells need kept constant:
Variable Regulated by (cross-ref)

pHLungs + kidneys (acid-base)

Osmolality/waterADH + thirst

The point: each of these has a set point (the target value) and a control system that corrects deviations — and every regulatory note you've built is one of these systems.
The Negative Feedback Loop — the core mechanism
Almost all homeostasis works by negative feedback — the response opposes the change, pulling the variable back toward the set point. Every feedback system has three components:
Component Role Example (temperature)
Sensor (receptor)Detects the changeThermoreceptors
Control centreCompares to the set point, coordinates the responseHypothalamus
EffectorProduces the corrective responseSweating/shivering, vasodilation/constriction
The logic (negative feedback): a deviation from the set point → detected → triggers a response that opposes/reverses the deviation → the variable returns toward normal → the response switches off. The response counteracts the stimulus (hence "negative").
The universality point (high-yield): this is the same structure as every regulatory system — e.g. ↑blood glucose → (sensor: β-cells) → insulin → (effector: cells take up glucose) → glucose falls; ↑BP → (baroreceptors) → ↓sympathetic → ↓BP; ↑cortisol → suppresses CRH/ACTH (the endocrine axes) → all the same negative-feedback logic.
Positive Feedback — the exception (high-yield)
Positive feedback amplifies the change (the response reinforces the stimulus) → not for maintaining stability, but for driving a process rapidly to completion:
Example The amplifying loop
The LH surge → ovulationOestrogen peak → ↑LH → more oestrogen → ovulation (cross-ref menstrual cycle)
Blood clottingActivated factors activate more factors (the cascade)
Labour/uterine contractionsContractions → ↑oxytocin → stronger contractions → delivery
The action potential upstrokeDepolarisation → opens Na⁺ channels → more depolarisation (cross-ref neuron/AP)
The key distinction (high-yield): negative feedback = stability (the norm); positive feedback = amplification to an endpoint (the rare exceptions) — the few positive-feedback loops (LH surge, clotting, labour, the AP upstroke) are worth knowing precisely because they're exceptions.

  • Feedforward control: the body sometimes anticipates a change before it happens (e.g. the cephalic phase of digestion — seeing food triggers acid/insulin release before eating; the anticipatory ↑ heart rate before exercise) → prepares in advance rather than just correcting after

Set points can be reset: e.g. fever — infection resets the hypothalamic temperature set point higher (pyrogens) → the body actively defends the new higher temperature (why you shiver with a fever).
Disease as failure of homeostasis (the key clinical concept): many diseases are a breakdown of homeostatic control:

HypertensionDysregulated BP control

The maladaptive-compensation point (high-yield): sometimes the homeostatic response itself becomes harmful — e.g. in heart failure, RAAS activation (a normal "low perfusion" response) causes fluid retention that worsens the failure → a homeostatic loop turned pathological (cross-ref heart failure/RAAS).

Overview — Basic Genetics & Inheritance
Genetics is the molecular basis of inheritance — how information is stored (DNA), expressed (→ protein), and passed on — and how variations cause inherited disease.
The organising principle: genetic information flows DNA → RNA → protein (the central dogma); it's packaged into chromosomes and inherited in predictable patterns (dominant, recessive, X-linked); mutations disrupt this and cause disease. Recognising the inheritance pattern predicts recurrence risk and which relatives are affected.
Why it matters: underpins inherited disease (cystic fibrosis, sickle cell, Huntington's, haemophilia), genetic counselling, the inheritance patterns, and pharmacogenomics — cross-ref the specific inherited conditions across your modules (CF, sickle cell, thalassaemia, Huntington's, haemophilia), drug biotransformation (pharmacogenomics).

The key concepts: genes code for proteins; the sequence of DNA bases → the sequence of amino acids → the protein's structure/function → so a mutation in the DNA → an altered protein → disease.
Chromosomes: humans have 46 (23 pairs) — 22 autosomal pairs + 1 sex pair (XX female, XY male); one of each pair from each parent.

Overview — Immunity (Active & Passive)
Immunity splits first into innate (born with it, non-specific, immediate, no memory) vs adaptive (acquired, specific, slower first time but has memory). This note focuses on the adaptive arm, whose decisive fork is active vs passive — the whole topic hangs on a 2×2 (active/passive × natural/artificial).
The defining trade-off: active = slow onset but long-lasting (memory); passive = immediate but short-lived (no memory).
Cross-ref: Immune System Overview & Immunodeficiency (fuller cellular immunology + deficiency syndromes), Vaccinations & Immunisation Schedule (artificial active immunity in practice), hypersensitivity (IgE).

How the two arms interact (high-yield): they’re not separate — antigen-presenting cells (dendritic cells, macrophages) bridge innate → adaptive: they detect the pathogen (innate) and present its antigen to T-cells → activating the specific response. In return, adaptive antibodies enhance innate function (opsonisation → better phagocytosis; complement activation). The fast innate response also buys time for the slower adaptive one to develop.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Antimic:
Overview — Antimicrobial Stewardship (AMS)
AMS = the coordinated effort to promote and monitor the responsible use of antimicrobials to preserve their future effectiveness — a public-health and patient-safety strategy, not a clinical condition.
The driving problem it addresses = antimicrobial resistance (AMR) — a global threat (projected ~10 million deaths/year by 2050) driven substantially by inappropriate antibiotic use.
The spine
Why AMR happens → the goals of stewardship → how it's done (Start Smart Then Focus) → resistance mechanisms.
Cross-ref: sepsis (empirical→targeted antibiotics), infective diarrhoea / C. diff (a consequence of broad-spectrum overuse), infection control / HAI, the antibiotics — mechanisms/classes note.
The Goals of Stewardship
Promote judicious antibiotic use to:
  • Reduce inappropriate use
  • Improve patient outcomes
  • Increase guideline adherence
  • Decrease resistance
  • Reduce healthcare costs
The balance it strikes: safeguard the quality of care for the patient in front of you while protecting antibiotics for future patients — the individual-vs-population tension is the conceptual heart.
Why AMR Develops
📷 Image placeholder — The 4 Cs driving C. difficile — Cephalosporins, Co-amoxiclav, Ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolones) and Clindamycin
Drivers of resistance
  • Over-prescribing (incl. for viral infections)
  • Broad-spectrum use when narrow would do
  • Inadequate dosing/duration, poor adherence
  • Agricultural antibiotic use, global spread
Consequences of resistance
  • Untreatable infections, longer admissions, higher mortality
  • Reliance on toxic/last-line agents
  • C. difficile and MRSA emergence from broad-spectrum overuse
The principle: every antibiotic exposure exerts selection pressure favouring resistant organisms — so the goal is "the right drug, for the right bug, at the right dose, for the right duration".
Start Smart, Then Focus — the UK framework
📷 Image placeholder — Start Smart Then Focus — start smart (document indication + review date, sample before antibiotics where it won’t delay) → review at 48–72h → Stop / Switch IV→oral / Change / Continue / OPAT
The two-phase model (UKHSA / NICE NG15) applied to every antibiotic prescription.
Phase 1 — START SMART (at initiation)
  • Don't start without clinical evidence of infection (avoid treating contamination/colonisation/viral illness)
  • Take cultures before starting (esp. blood cultures — cross-ref sepsis)
  • Follow local prescribing guidelines (reflecting local resistance patterns)
  • Document: indication, drug, dose, route, and a review/stop date on the chart
  • Consider severity, immunocompromise, resistance risk, and prior antibiotic exposure
Phase 2 — THEN FOCUS (the antibiotic review at 48–72 h)
Review the diagnosis and continuing need at 48–72 hours, and document a clear plan — one of five outcomes:
Outcome Action
StopNo evidence of infection → cease
SwitchIV → oral (when stable)
ChangeDe-escalate to a narrower-spectrum agent (or broaden if needed) per culture results
ContinueDocument review date
OPATOutpatient parenteral antibiotic therapy
De-escalation (empirical broad-spectrum → narrow targeted once sensitivities return) is the pivotal AMS action.
Practical Stewardship Measures
The "right" mnemonic: right drug, dose, route, duration, for the right diagnosis.
  • IV-to-oral switch as soon as appropriate (reduces line infections, length of stay)
  • Shortest effective duration (the old "always finish the course" dogma is dropped where evidence supports shorter courses)
  • Narrowest effective spectrum; reserve last-line agents (carbapenems, vancomycin) via restriction/approval
  • Cultures before antibiotics; use biomarkers (e.g. procalcitonin) to guide stopping where available
  • AMS teams (microbiologist + antimicrobial pharmacist), local guidelines, audit/feedback, prescriber education, ward rounds
  • Public/prescriber education: antibiotics don't treat viral infections; delayed prescribing in primary care
Mechanisms of Resistance
Mechanism Example
Altered targetRNA polymerase (rifampicin), DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin), 30S ribosome (streptomycin)
Alternative targetAltered penicillin-binding protein in MRSA
Drug modification / breakdownβ-lactamases (penicillins), aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes
Efflux pumpsTetracyclines, quinolones, β-lactams
MRSA = the archetype: Staph aureus resistant to β-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via altered PBP → treated with doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, or linezolid.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Pyrexia:
Overview — Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO)
PUO is not a disease but a diagnostic problem: a prolonged fever that remains undiagnosed despite a proper initial workup. The topic is about a structured approach to a defined differential, not a single condition.
The spine
Define it → place the patient in the right sub-type → work through the four cause-buckets → investigate in a staged, history-led way.
The decisive feature is the precise definition (Petersdorf & Beeson) — the "3 weeks + appropriate investigation" separates true PUO from an ordinary acute fever and narrows the likely causes.
Cross-ref: sepsis (the acute febrile patient — PUO is the chronic counterpart), TB / infective endocarditis / lymphoma / GCA (classic causes), HIV (a sub-type and a cause), notifiable diseases (some causes notifiable).
Definition — Petersdorf & Beeson
Element Criterion
Temperature>38.3°C on several occasions
DurationFever persisting ≥3 weeks
InvestigationNo diagnosis despite appropriate workup — originally 1 week inpatient, now revised to 3 outpatient visits or 3 days of inpatient / intensive ambulatory investigation
Why "≥3 weeks + investigated" matters: by definition these patients have already resisted classification on baseline investigation, so the differential is a specific (often smaller, often serious) set — most self-limiting viral fevers have resolved or declared themselves by 3 weeks.
The Four Sub-types — establish which first

The principle: establish the sub-type first — it reshapes the differential and the urgency (neutropenic PUO is an emergency; classic PUO is a methodical workup).
Causes — the Four Buckets
Bucket Examples
Infection (large group, esp. developing world)TB (esp. miliary/extrapulmonary — the classic PUO cause), occult abscess (subphrenic, pelvic, dental), infective endocarditis, osteomyelitis, HIV, EBV/CMV, brucellosis, hidden empyema
MalignancyLymphoma (the classic), leukaemia, renal cell carcinoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, atrial myxoma

The reality: infection predominates in developing nations, non-infectious inflammatory disease in industrialised nations — and a large proportion (up to ~half in some series) remain undiagnosed despite full workup (many resolve spontaneously, a reassuring point).
The classic don't-miss trio: TB, lymphoma, and giant cell arteritis (GCA especially in the elderly — treatable, sight-threatening).
Assessment — history + examination drive the workup
History — the highest-yield step
  • Fever pattern/duration; travel (malaria, typhoid, TB)
  • Animal/occupational exposure (brucellosis, Q fever); sexual history (HIV); drug history (drug fever)
  • TB risk/contacts; weight loss / night sweats (B symptoms → lymphoma/TB)
  • Joint/skin/eye symptoms (connective tissue); family history (FMF); recent surgery/lines (nosocomial)
Examination — repeated and thorough: a meticulous, repeated examination is essential — new signs (a murmur, lymphadenopathy, a rash, temporal artery tenderness, splenomegaly) often emerge over time and provide the diagnostic lead.
Red flags
Weight loss + night sweats (malignancy/TB), new murmur (endocarditis), localising signs, immunocompromise/neutropenia (urgent).
Investigations — staged, escalating, history-led
📷 Image placeholder — Tiered PUO workup — first-line bloods/cultures/CXR → second-line CT and echo (TTE→TOE) → third-line PET-CT/biopsy
First-line (baseline)
FBC + film, U&E, LFT, CRP/ESR, blood cultures (×3 from 3 different sites, before antibiotics), urinalysis + culture, CXR, HIV test, autoantibodies (ANA, ANCA, RF), TFTs, LDH, blood film for malaria if travel.
Second-line (directed)
CT chest/abdomen/pelvis (occult abscess, lymphadenopathy, malignancy), echocardiography (endocarditis — TTE → TOE), viral serology (EBV, CMV, hepatitis), TB workup (sputum, IGRA, biopsy), tumour markers.
Third-line (specialist)
PET-CT (increasingly useful for occult malignancy/inflammation/infection), biopsy (lymph node, bone marrow, temporal artery, liver), invasive imaging.
The governing principle: investigate logically and in a directed way — let history and examination steer the next test rather than ordering everything at once. Avoid empirical "blind" antibiotics/steroids unless the patient is unstable, as they obscure the diagnosis.
Management
Treat the underlying cause once found — PUO itself isn't treated, the diagnosis is.
Avoid blind empirical treatment (antibiotics/steroids) in the stable patient — it masks the picture. Exceptions: neutropenic/immunocompromised (urgent empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics), strong suspicion of GCA (urgent steroids to prevent blindness), or clinical instability/sepsis.
A significant proportion resolve spontaneously undiagnosed — careful follow-up rather than ever-more-invasive testing is appropriate in the stable, improving patient.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Travel:
Overview — Travel Medicine / Malaria Prophylaxis
Two linked jobs: the pre-travel consultation (risk assessment, vaccines, advice) and specifically malaria prophylaxis (the most examinable part).
The organising framework — ABCD
  • Awareness of risk
  • Bite prevention
  • Chemoprophylaxis
  • Diagnose promptly (treat any fever after travel as malaria until proven otherwise)
The single most important safety message: no prophylaxis is 100% effective — any fever during or after travel to an endemic area is malaria until proven otherwise, and bite avoidance matters as much as the drugs.
Cross-ref: infective diarrhoea (travellers' diarrhoea), vaccinations, notifiable diseases (malaria, typhoid, VHF, yellow fever are notifiable).
The Pre-Travel Consultation
📷 Image placeholder — Yellow fever — a LIVE vaccine, single dose now gives a lifelong certificate; contraindicated in immunosuppression and infants <9 months, cautioned in pregnancy/egg allergy
  • Risk assessment: destination, rural vs urban, duration, season, activities, accommodation; patient factors (age, pregnancy, immunosuppression, comorbidities, current meds)
  • Travel vaccines (cross-ref schedule): routine boosters + destination-specific — hepatitis A, typhoid, yellow fever (certificate may be legally required for entry), rabies, Japanese encephalitis, cholera, meningococcal ACWY (e.g. Hajj)
  • General advice: food/water hygiene (travellers' diarrhoea), sun/heat, accident/road-traffic risk (the commonest cause of traveller death), STI/blood-borne risk, travel insurance
Bite avoidance — the "B", applies to all
DEET repellent, covering skin at dawn/dusk, insecticide-treated bed nets, air conditioning.
Malaria Background — enough to make prophylaxis make sense
  • Caused by Plasmodium (mosquito-borne, Anopheles); five species, but P. falciparum = the deadly one (cerebral malaria, the bulk of travel deaths)
  • P. vivax and P. ovale have a dormant liver stage (hypnozoites) → they can relapse months later even after correct prophylaxis (the key to understanding primaquine)
The crucial mechanism point: standard prophylactic drugs (chloroquine, mefloquine, doxycycline, atovaquone-proguanil) are "suppressive" — they act on the blood stage, NOT on initial infection or liver hypnozoites. This is why they must be continued for 4 weeks after leaving (to cover parasites emerging from the liver), and why vivax/ovale can still relapse.

The "4 weeks after" vs "1 week after" rule: only atovaquone-proguanil stops at 1 week (it hits the liver stage); the suppressive agents (doxycycline, mefloquine, chloroquine) need 4 weeks to cover emerging blood-stage parasites.
Selection logic: atovaquone-proguanil and doxycycline are first-choice for most (best tolerated); mefloquine's neuropsychiatric profile makes it the one to avoid in psychiatric/epilepsy history, but its weekly dose suits long trips. Choice also depends on the resistance pattern of the destination, cost, pregnancy, and tolerability.
Special Situations
📷 Image placeholder — If chloroquine + proguanil is used in pregnancy, co-prescribe folic acid 5 mg daily (proguanil is a folate antagonist)

Malaria is more severe in pregnancy; mefloquine can be used; chloroquine + proguanil where appropriate; doxycycline is contraindicated; atovaquone-proguanil generally avoided (verify against current UK guidance).
Relapse prevention (P. vivax / ovale)
Primaquine is the only drug acting on liver hypnozoites — used as presumptive anti-relapse therapy after significant exposure; must check G6PD first (primaquine → haemolysis in G6PD deficiency).
Children, immunocompromised, long-term travellers
Individualised, specialist advice.
Diagnose Promptly — the "D", the can't-miss
Any febrile illness during or up to a year after travel to an endemic area = malaria until excluded.
  • Diagnosis: thick and thin blood films (thick = detect parasites, thin = speciate + quantify) — three negative films over 48 h to exclude; rapid antigen tests as adjunct
  • Falciparum is a medical emergency → urgent treatment
  • Malaria is a notifiable disease (cross-ref)

Overview — Infective Diarrhoea (Gastroenteritis)
GI infection causing diarrhoea ± vomiting — mostly self-limiting and managed with rehydration. The skill examined is recognising the specific organisms by their clinical signatures and knowing the few that change management.
Fork 1 — Bloody vs non-bloody
Inflammatory / invasive (bloody) vs secretory / watery (non-bloody).
Fork 2 — Antibiotics or not
The highest-yield rule: never give antibiotics if E. coli O157 (Shiga-toxin) is possible — they increase HUS risk.
Cross-ref: HUS (the E. coli O157 complication — AKI subtab), notifiable diseases (most are notifiable), infection control, C. difficile (antibiotic-associated), IBD (the non-infective differential).

The Three Named Organisms — in detail
Campylobacter — the commonest bacterial cause
  • Gram-negative, curved/spiral rod; commonest bacterial gastroenteritis worldwide; from undercooked poultry, untreated water, unpasteurised milk; common travellers' diarrhoea
  • Incubation 2–5 days; resolves in 3–6 days: abdo cramps (can mimic appendicitis), bloody diarrhoea, fever
  • Antibiotics only after isolating the organism if severe or high-risk (immunocompromised, HIV, heart failure): clarithromycin first-line (azithromycin / ciprofloxacin alternatives)
  • Sequelae (high-yield): Guillain-Barré syndrome and reactive arthritis
E. coli O157:H7 (STEC) — the one that changes management
  • Produces Shiga toxin → abdominal cramps, bloody diarrhoea, vomiting; the toxin destroys red blood cells → haemolytic uraemic syndrome (HUS)
  • THE RULE: antibiotics increase the risk of HUS → avoid antibiotics if E. coli O157 is possible (the single most-tested fact in this topic)
  • HUS triad (cross-ref AKI subtab): AKI + microangiopathic haemolytic anaemia + thrombocytopenia — commonest in children, ~6% of O157 infections
  • Source: undercooked beef, unpasteurised dairy, petting farms
Salmonella
  • From eggs, poultry, raw foods; incubation 12–48 h; watery (± bloody) diarrhoea, cramps, fever, vomiting
  • Usually self-limiting; antibiotics only if severe/invasive or high-risk (risk of prolonging carriage); can cause bacteraemia and reactive arthritis
  • Distinct from typhoid / enteric fever (Salmonella typhi) — a systemic illness
Clinical Assessment
  • History: onset/duration, blood in stool, vomiting, food / travel / contact history, antibiotic use (C. diff), immunosuppression
Assess dehydration — the main thing that matters: dry mucous membranes, reduced skin turgor, tachycardia, hypotension, reduced urine output, prolonged CRT. The priority assessment in the unwell patient.
Red flags
  • Bloody diarrhoea, high fever
  • Signs of HUS (reduced urine / pallor / bruising)
  • Severe dehydration / shock, immunocompromise, recent hospital / antibiotics (C. diff)
Investigations
Most cases need no investigation — self-limiting, clinical diagnosis.
  • Stool MC&S (+ ova/cysts/parasites) if: bloody diarrhoea, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, recent travel, suspected outbreak, or symptoms >7 days
  • Stool Shiga-toxin / E. coli O157 testing if bloody (informs the no-antibiotics decision)
  • C. diff toxin if recent antibiotics
  • Bloods if unwell: FBC (HUS — anaemia + thrombocytopenia + film for schistocytes), U&E (AKI + dehydration), CRP, cultures if septic
Management — rehydration is the mainstay

Rehydration = the cornerstone: oral rehydration solution first-line; IV fluids if severe dehydration / shock / vomiting (cross-ref fluid therapy).
Supportive
  • Antiemetics if needed
  • Avoid antimotility agents (loperamide) in bloody / inflammatory diarrhoea — risk of toxic megacolon and prolonged toxin exposure
Antibiotics — the selective approach
  • NOT routine — most self-limiting; antibiotics can prolong carriage or precipitate HUS
  • AVOID entirely if E. coli O157 possible (↑HUS)
  • Consider for: severe campylobacter/shigella, systemically unwell, immunocompromised, specific organisms (giardia → metronidazole, C. diff → vancomycin/fidaxomicin)
Public health
  • Most are notifiable
  • Infection control: isolate, hand hygiene — alcohol gel ineffective against C. diff / norovirus → soap and water
  • Exclusion from work/school until 48 h symptom-free (especially food handlers)
Complications
HUS (E. coli O157, Shigella — the can't-miss; don't give antibiotics) · Guillain-Barré, reactive arthritis (post-campylobacter) · dehydration / AKI / shock · bacteraemia (Salmonella) · toxic megacolon · post-infectious IBS · C. diff colitis.

Pattern recognition
Bloody = invasive (Campylobacter, E. coli O157, Salmonella, Shigella); fast onset (1–6 h) = preformed toxin (Staph aureus, B. cereus "fried rice").
Campylobacter
Commonest bacterial, poultry/travel; → Guillain-Barré + reactive arthritis; clarithromycin if treating.
E. coli O157 — the key rule
Shiga toxin → HUS; NEVER give antibiotics if O157 possible (↑HUS).
HUS triad
AKI + MAHA + thrombocytopenia (children; cross-ref AKI).
Management
Rehydration is the mainstay (ORS → IV); avoid loperamide in bloody diarrhoea.
When to investigate
Stool MC&S if bloody / unwell / travel / immunocompromised / >7 days; Shiga-toxin test if bloody.
Public health
Most notifiable; soap and water (not alcohol gel) for C. diff / norovirus; food handlers excluded until 48 h clear.
Giardia
Chronic fatty diarrhoea after travel → metronidazole.
INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Meningo:
Overview — Meningococcal Disease
📷 Image placeholder — Gram stain — Gram-negative diplococci (Neisseria meningitidis)
Meningococcal disease = invasive infection with Neisseria meningitidis (a Gram-negative diplococcus) — a medical emergency.
Meningococcal meningitis
N. meningitidis infects the meninges + CSF → the meningitic picture.
Meningococcal septicaemia
The bacteria invade the bloodstream → non-blanching rash + shock — the more lethal form.
The single most important action: suspected meningococcal disease in the community → urgent IM/IV benzylpenicillin and immediate transfer — do not wait.
Cross-ref: sepsis / shock (septicaemia → septic shock + DIC), notifiable diseases (it is notifiable), vaccinations (Men B / ACWY in the schedule).
Meningitis vs Septicaemia — the spine
Meningococcal meningitis Meningococcal septicaemia
SiteMeninges + CSFBloodstream
Dominant featuresHeadache, neck stiffness, photophobia, feverNon-blanching petechial/purpuric rash, shock
Key dangerRaised ICP, neuro damageSeptic shock, DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen
The rashMay be absentThe classic feature (but can be absent)
The non-blanching rash is caused by the septicaemia; it can be absent in meningococcal disease — its absence never excludes the diagnosis.
The Other Causes of Meningitis — the differential
Bacterial — by age
  • Neonates → Group B Strep, E. coli, Listeria
  • Children / adults → N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae
  • Elderly / immunocompromised / pregnant → add Listeria
Viral — commonest overall, usually milder
Enteroviruses, HSV, VZV.
Meningococcus + pneumococcus = the two big bacterial causes in the immunocompetent child/adult.
Clinical Features
📷 Image placeholder — Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash with a positive glass/tumbler test — the spots do not fade under pressure (septicaemic picture)
Meningitic picture
  • Classic triad = fever + neck stiffness + altered mental status (present in only ~60% — its absence doesn't exclude it)
  • Headache, photophobia, vomiting
  • Meningism signs: Kernig's (pain on knee extension with hip flexed), Brudzinski's (involuntary hip/knee flexion on neck flexion)
Septicaemic picture
  • Non-blanching petechial/purpuric rash — the glass/tumbler test (doesn't fade under pressure)
  • Cold peripheries, limb pain
  • Signs of shock: tachycardia, hypotension, prolonged CRT
Babies / young children — atypical, easily missed
Non-specific: fever, lethargy, poor feeding, bulging fontanelle, high-pitched cry, hypotonia, seizures.
Red flags for raised ICP (contraindicate LP): reduced/fluctuating GCS, focal neurology, seizures, papilloedema, bradycardia + hypertension.
Investigations — don't let them delay treatment
  • Blood: cultures, meningococcal PCR (key confirmatory test — remains positive after antibiotics), FBC, U&E, CRP, glucose, clotting (DIC), lactate, ABG
  • Lumbar puncture + CSF analysis — ideally before antibiotics, but never delay antibiotics in an acutely unwell patient; contraindicated if raised ICP / shock / coagulopathy (do CT + treat first)
CSF interpretation — bacterial vs viral
Bacterial Viral
AppearanceCloudy / turbidClear
Cells↑↑ neutrophils↑ lymphocytes
ProteinHighNormal / mildly raised
Glucose (CSF:plasma)Low (<½ plasma)Normal
Bacteria release proteins and consume glucose (→ high protein, low glucose); the immune system sends neutrophils to bacteria, lymphocytes to viruses. TB / fungal meningitis: lymphocytes + high protein + low glucose.
Management — the time-critical pathway
Community / pre-hospital: suspected meningococcal disease (especially a non-blanching rash) → urgent IM/IV benzylpenicillin (or IM ceftriaxone); for suspected meningitis without a rash, transfer immediately without delaying, while awaiting transfer — but it must NOT delay transfer; in true penicillin allergy, prioritise transfer.
Hospital — empirical antibiotics
  • Ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime) = the mainstay third-generation cephalosporin
  • Add amoxicillin if Listeria risk (neonates, >50, immunocompromised, pregnant)
  • Add vancomycin if recent travel / penicillin-resistant pneumococcus risk
Dexamethasone: reduces complications, particularly hearing loss in bacterial meningitis (esp. pneumococcal) — given with / just before antibiotics.
  • Supportive: treat septic shock (Sepsis Six, fluids, vasopressors — cross-ref sepsis), manage raised ICP, correct DIC
  • Duration: meningococcal meningitis → ceftriaxone (or cefotaxime), a short course (~5–7 days) for uncomplicated recovery
  • Don't forget: notifiable disease → inform public health / UKHSA immediately
Contact Prophylaxis — the public-health arm
Close contacts (household, kissing contacts, same-room exposure) need post-exposure prophylaxis to eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage.
  • Ciprofloxacin (single dose — now first-line, suits all ages + pregnancy) or rifampicin
  • Notify UKHSA, who coordinate contact tracing + prophylaxis
  • Vaccination of contacts if a vaccine-preventable serogroup
Complications
📷 Image placeholder — Purpura fulminans with peripheral/digital ischaemia in meningococcal septicaemia (DIC-driven) — the route to limb/digit loss
Acute
  • Septic shock + DIC
  • Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome (bilateral adrenal haemorrhage → adrenal failure)
  • Raised ICP / cerebral oedema, seizures, death
Chronic / sequelae
  • Sensorineural hearing loss (commonest — hence dexamethasone)
  • Neurodevelopmental delay, epilepsy, focal neurology
  • Limb / digit loss (purpura fulminans / ischaemia)
Prevention
  • Vaccination (cross-ref vaccination schedule): Men B (infants), Men ACWY (teenagers/students), Hib/Men C
  • Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (above)
⭐ Exam Pearls
The organism
N. meningitidis = Gram-negative diplococcus; meningitis (meninges) + septicaemia (blood → non-blanching rash), often together.
The rash
Non-blanching = septicaemia (glass test), but can be absent — never exclude on rash alone.
Clinical signs
Classic triad (fever + neck stiffness + altered mental state) in only ~60%; Kernig's / Brudzinski's; babies → bulging fontanelle, lethargy.
Community first action
IM benzylpenicillin + transfer NOW — don't delay.
Hospital antibiotics
Ceftriaxone + dexamethasone (+ amoxicillin if Listeria risk: neonate / >50 / pregnant / immunocompromised).
CSF
Bacterial = cloudy, ↑neutrophils, ↑protein, ↓glucose; viral = clear, lymphocytes, normal glucose. LP contraindicated if raised ICP / shock.
Confirmation
Meningococcal PCR — positive even after antibiotics.
Public health
Notifiable disease → UKHSA; close contacts → ciprofloxacin prophylaxis.
Complications
DIC, Waterhouse-Friderichsen (adrenal haemorrhage), hearing loss (dexamethasone reduces it).
INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Sepsis:
Overview — Sepsis
Sepsis = life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection (Sepsis-3). It is not the infection itself but the body's damaging reaction to it — a time-critical emergency where every hour of delayed antibiotics increases mortality.
The spine of this note: recognise early → deliver the Sepsis Six within 1 hour → identify and control the source.
The severity ladder
Infection  →  Sepsis (organ dysfunction)  →  Septic shock (refractory hypotension + raised lactate)
Cross-ref: shock (septic shock is a distributive shock — the DOCH framework), AKI (a common organ dysfunction), antimicrobial stewardship (empirical → targeted), and the specific sources — pneumonia, UTI/pyelonephritis, cholangitis, cellulitis, meningococcal disease.
Definitions — the Sepsis-3 hierarchy
📷 Image placeholder — Severity ladder — infection → sepsis (organ dysfunction) → septic shock (vasopressor-requiring hypotension + lactate >2 despite fluids)
Term Definition
SepsisLife-threatening organ dysfunction from a dysregulated host response to infection
Septic shockSepsis with persisting hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65 + lactate >2 despite adequate fluid resuscitation
BacteraemiaBacteria in the blood (≠ sepsis — may be transient/harmless)
SIRS — the older systemic-inflammatory-response criteria — has been superseded by Sepsis-3's organ-dysfunction focus, but still appears as a screening tool.
Pathophysiology — why a dysregulated response causes shock
  • Infection → release of pathogen-associated molecular patterns (PAMPs) → massive innate immune activation → cytokine storm (the dysregulation)
  • → widespread vasodilation + capillary leak (NO-mediated) → distributive ("warm") shock (cross-ref shock note)
  • → microvascular thrombosis + endothelial injury → tissue hypoperfusion → lactate rises (anaerobic metabolism) → multi-organ dysfunction
  • → DIC (consumption of clotting factors), AKI, ARDS, encephalopathy
Risk Factors — who is vulnerable
  • Extremes of age (very young, elderly)
  • Immunocompromise — chemotherapy, steroids, diabetes, HIV, asplenia
  • Indwelling devices — lines, catheters
  • Recent surgery / instrumentation
  • Pregnancy / peripartum
  • IVDU, chronic disease
Recognition & Screening
Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis — no single test rules it in or out.
Score Use Note
NEWS2The preferred in-hospital screening tool2026 Surviving Sepsis recommends NEWS2/NEWS/MEWS/SIRS over qSOFA — track-and-trigger, most sensitive
qSOFAQuick bedside (≥2 = high risk)GCS <15, RR ≥22, SBP ≤100; no longer recommended as a sole screening tool — less sensitive than EWS
SIRSOlder criteriaTemp, HR, RR, WCC derangement
Practical update: qSOFA is being de-emphasised as a screening tool in favour of NEWS2 (2026 guideline shift); it remains useful as a predictor of poor outcome.
Red flags prompting urgent action
  • Altered mentation; SBP ≤90 (or drop >40 from baseline); RR ≥25
  • SpO₂ needing O₂; lactate >2; reduced urine output
  • Mottled / ashen skin; non-blanching rash
The Sepsis Six — deliver within 1 hour ("take 3, give 3")
📷 Image placeholder — The Sepsis Six one-hour bundle — TAKE 3 (blood cultures, lactate, urine output) and GIVE 3 (oxygen, IV broad-spectrum antibiotics, IV fluids)
GIVE 3 TAKE 3
1. Oxygen — target 94–98% (88–92% if COPD retainer)1. Blood cultures (before antibiotics)
2. IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (empirical, per local guidelines)2. Lactate (via VBG/ABG)
3. IV fluids (balanced crystalloid bolus, e.g. 500 mL, reassess)3. Urine output (catheterise + monitor, aim >0.5 mL/kg/h)
Antibiotic timing is the single most important intervention: give broad-spectrum antibiotics immediately, ideally within 1 hour, for septic shock or high-likelihood sepsis. Take blood cultures before antibiotics where possible — but do not delay antibiotics for them in shock.
Fluids: use dynamic measures to guide resuscitation; reassess after each bolus — avoid both under- and over-resuscitation.
Source Control — the principle often forgotten
📷 Image placeholder — Source-to-intervention map — abscess → drainage, obstructed infected kidney → nephrostomy/stent, cholangitis → ERCP, infected line → remove, necrotising fasciitis/perforation → surgery, empyema → chest drain
Antibiotics alone are not enough if there is a focus of infection that needs physical removal or drainage. Source control is the definitive step — a collection of pus under pressure will not clear with antibiotics alone.
Source Source control
AbscessDrainage (radiological or surgical)
Obstructed + infected kidneyNephrostomy / stent (cross-ref renal calculi)
Ascending cholangitisERCP biliary decompression (cross-ref)
Infected line / deviceRemove it
Necrotising fasciitis / perforationUrgent surgical debridement / repair
EmpyemaChest drain
The principle: find the source and control it — the same logic as the cholangitis and infected-stone notes.
Further Management & Escalation
  • Reassess after the Sepsis Six: repeat lactate; if not improving → escalate to HDU/ICU
  • Septic shock: fluid-refractory hypotension → vasopressors (noradrenaline first-line) to maintain MAP ≥65 (cross-ref shock)
  • De-escalate antibiotics once cultures/sensitivities return (empirical → targeted — cross-ref stewardship)
  • Treat organ dysfunction: AKI (may need RRT), ARDS (ventilation), DIC
Complications
Septic shock, multi-organ dysfunction (AKI, ARDS, hepatic, encephalopathy), DIC, death. Long-term: post-sepsis syndrome (physical / cognitive impairment).

Sepsis = organ dysfunction from a dysregulated response to infection; septic shock = vasopressor-requiring hypotension + lactate >2 despite fluids.

Distributive ("warm") shock — vasodilation + capillary leak (cross-ref shock note).

"Take 3, give 3": cultures / lactate / urine output + oxygen / antibiotics / fluids.

The key mortality intervention; cultures before antibiotics (but don't delay in shock).

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Immune:
Overview — Immune System & Immunodeficiency
Immunodeficiency = a missing or defective component of the immune system → recurrent, severe, unusual, or persistent infections.
The single organising principle: the deficient component predicts the infection pattern — work out which arm has failed, and you predict the bug.
The structure
  • Top-level fork = primary (genetic/intrinsic) vs secondary (acquired) — secondary is far commoner
  • Four functional arms that can fail: humoral (B-cell/antibody), cell-mediated (T-cell), phagocyte, complement
Cross-ref the Immunity note for the fuller innate/adaptive overview, Ig classes, and interleukins.
The Organising Principle — read this first
Deficient arm Characteristic infections The clue
Humoral (B-cell/antibody)Encapsulated bacteria — H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis ("SHiN")Recurrent sinopulmonary infections, after 6 months of age
T-cell (cell-mediated)"HIV-type" opportunists — viruses, fungi (PCP/candida), intracellular bacteria (TB), protozoaSevere/atypical viral + fungal infections
PhagocyteCatalase-positive bacteria (Staph aureus) + fungi (Aspergillus)Abscesses, osteomyelitis, in childhood
ComplementNeisseria (recurrent meningococcal)Recurrent meningococcaemia
Primary vs Secondary
Primary (intrinsic/genetic)
The named syndromes — XLA, DiGeorge, CGD, SCID, etc. (below).
Secondary (acquired — commoner)
HIV (the big one), drugs (steroids, rituximab, cytotoxics, natalizumab), malignancy (myeloma, leukaemia/lymphoma, CLL), protein loss (nephrotic, PLE), malnutrition, asplenia/hyposplenism, diabetes, extremes of age.
Brief Immune Recap — the scaffold
  • Innate (non-specific, rapid): granulocytes (neutrophils → bacteria; eosinophils → parasites/allergy; basophils → allergy), APCs (dendritic cells, macrophages), NK cells (kill intracellular pathogens via perforins/granzymes), complement
  • Adaptive (specific, memory): T-cells — CD4+ (helper), CD8+ (cytotoxic), T-reg (suppress); B-cells (antibodies)
MHC & the Rule of 8: Class I (HLA-A/B/C, all nucleated cells → CD8 + NK; CD8 × MHC I = 8); Class II (HLA-DQ/DR/DP, APCs + B-cells only → CD4; CD4 × MHC II = 8).
TH1 vs TH2
  • TH1 (cell-mediated): IL-12 → TH1 → IFNγ → macrophage activation → IL-1/6/8, TNFα
  • TH2 (humoral): IL-4 → TH2; IL-4 → IgE + B-cell proliferation, IL-5 → IgA + eosinophils, IL-10 → inhibits TH1
Complement function
C3/4/5a = anaphylatoxins (mast cell degranulation); C3b = opsonisation (splenic phagocytosis); C5a = neutrophil chemotaxis; C5–9 = membrane attack complex (kills Neisseria).
Humoral (B-cell / Antibody) Deficits
  • X-Linked Agammaglobulinaemia (XLA / Bruton's): BTK mutation → absent B-cells + absent antibodies; presents after 6 months (maternal IgG wanes); recurrent URTI/LRTI with encapsulated organisms
  • Common Variable Immune Deficiency (CVID): like XLA but less severe (low rather than absent antibodies); affects adults; ↑risk of autoimmune disease and lymphoma
  • Selective IgA Deficiency: the most common primary immunodeficiency; GI/respiratory infections (esp. Giardia, Cryptosporidium); often asymptomatic; risk of anaphylaxis to blood products → give washed/IgA-deficient products if transfusing
Infection risk by antibody type: IgG deficiency → encapsulated bacteria (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis); IgA deficiency → GI/respiratory (Giardia, Cryptosporidium).
Secondary causes: nephrotic syndrome (antibody loss), myeloma, rituximab (anti-CD20), cytotoxics.
T-cell (Cell-Mediated) Deficits
DiGeorge Syndrome (22q11.2 deletion)
Loss of the 3rd/4th pharyngeal arch → thymic aplasia (↓T-cells) + hypoparathyroidism (↓PTH → hypocalcaemia); also cleft palate, conotruncal cardiac defects.
CATCH-22: Cardiac, Abnormal facies, Thymic aplasia, Cleft palate, Hypocalcaemia, 22q11.2. Tetany/hypocalcaemia at birth + cardiac defect → think DiGeorge.
Secondary: HIV/AIDS (destroys CD4+ — commonest acquired T-cell deficiency), natalizumab (blocks T-cell extravasation), cytotoxics.
Infections (think HIV): bacteria — Mycoplasma, TB, Salmonella, Listeria; viruses — herpesviruses (VZV, HSV, CMV, HHV8, EBV), HPV; fungi — Candida, Pneumocystis jirovecii (PCP), Histoplasma; protozoa — Cryptosporidium, Toxoplasma.
Phagocyte Deficits
  • Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD): X-linked; loss of NADPH oxidase → no respiratory burst → can't kill catalase-positive organisms (esp. Staph aureus, Aspergillus); presents before age 5 with osteomyelitis, abscesses, sepsis. Diagnosis: NBT (nitroblue tetrazolium) test fails to turn blue, or DHR flow cytometry
  • Chédiak-Higashi: lysosomal defect → dysfunctional phagocytosis + NK/CD8 → partial albinism + peripheral neuropathy + pancytopenia
  • Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency: CD18 mutation → impaired phagocyte migration → delayed umbilical cord separation, recurrent bacterial infections without pus
Complement Deficits
Complement defect Result

Combined Immunodeficiencies
  • SCID (Severe Combined Immunodeficiency): failure of both B and T cells — the "bubble baby"; causes = X-linked common gamma chain mutation (commonest), adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency; presents in infancy — FTT, persistent diarrhoea, chronic candidiasis, severe infections, disseminated infection from live vaccines (BCG, rotavirus); a paediatric emergency → stem cell transplant; avoid live vaccines (now on newborn screening)
  • Ataxia Telangiectasia: AR, ATM gene; "AAA" — Ataxia + Angiomas (telangiectasia) + Antibodies low (IgG/A/E); lymphopenia; ↑leukaemia/lymphoma; high radiation sensitivity
  • Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome: X-linked; "WATER" — Wiskott (thrombocytopenia) + Atopy (eczema) + T-cell dysfunction + Elevated IgE/A + Recurrent pyogenic infections (IgM/G low); eczema + thrombocytopenia + infections in a male = WAS

  • Hyper-IgE Syndrome (Job's): raised IgE + eosinophilia → atopy, weak bones (pathological fractures), cold Staph abscesses (no inflammatory signs); mnemonic FATED — coarse Facies, cold Abscesses, retained primary Teeth, raised IgE, Dermatological/eczema
Asplenia / Hyposplenism — the splenic angle
The spleen clears encapsulated organisms → asplenia (post-splenectomy, sickle cell autosplenectomy, coeliac) → risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) with encapsulated bacteria (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis).
  • Blood film clue: Howell-Jolly bodies
  • Management: vaccination (pneumococcal, Hib, MenACWY + MenB, annual influenza), lifelong prophylactic penicillin, patient alert card + education, prompt treatment of febrile illness

When to suspect — "SPUR": Severe, Persistent, Unusual (opportunistic organisms/sites), Recurrent; plus failure to thrive, family history, infection from live vaccines.

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Hyperse:
Overview — Hypersensitivity & Autoimmunity
Both halves = the immune system attacking the wrong target: hypersensitivity = an excessive/inappropriate immune response; autoimmunity = loss of self-tolerance so the immune system attacks the host.
The examinable spine for hypersensitivity = the Gell & Coombs classification — this course uses a five-type version (Types I–IV + Type V for receptor antibodies).
Cross-ref: the Immunity note (IgE/IL-4/IL-5, complement); the individual autoimmune diseases in their system notes (SLE→rheum, Graves'/Hashimoto's→endocrine, MG→neuro, Goodpasture's→renal); immunodeficiency (the neighbouring topic).
