Mnemonic — ABCD(E): Allergic (I), antibody/B cytotoxic (II), immune Complex (III), Delayed (IV), receptor (V). The core split: I–III + V = antibody-mediated; IV = T-cell-mediated/delayed (no antibody).
This course's classification choices (examined): Graves'/MG = Type V (not lumped into II); coeliac/Crohn's/MS/sarcoid = Type IV; post-strep GN = Type III.
Type I in Depth — Allergy, Anaphylaxis, Angioedema, Urticaria
Mechanism: IgE cross-linking → mast cell/basophil degranulation → histamine + leukotriene release (also via complement C3/4/5a, substance P, axon reflex). Examples: allergy (aspirin sensitivity, allergic rhinitis, atopy), anaphylaxis, angioedema, asthma, urticaria.
Anaphylaxis — the emergency
  • Anaphylaxis = IgE-mediated mast cell cross-linking; anaphylactoid = non-IgE degranulation (same treatment)
  • Presentation: angioedema, hypotension, bronchospasm/wheeze, urticaria (the ABC + skin picture)
  • Diagnosis: clinical + mast cell tryptase (serial levels confirm retrospectively)
Management: IM adrenaline 500 mcg (0.5 mL of 1:1000) — the key intervention, repeat every 5 min as needed; high-flow oxygen + IV fluids; adjuncts IV hydrocortisone 200 mg + chlorphenamine 10 mg (newer Resus Council guidance de-emphasises routine steroids/antihistamines acutely). Refractory → ICU; on discharge: observe + adrenaline auto-injector + allergy referral.
Angioedema
Subcutaneous/submucosal swelling ± urticaria; can be C1-esterase inhibitor deficiency (hereditary or acquired — autoimmune, haematological cancers, HepB/C). Acute (allergic) → treat as anaphylaxis; C1-INH-related → icatibant (bradykinin inhibitor); prevention → danazol, tranexamic acid, C1-esterase inhibitor.
Urticaria
Red, itchy dermal rash; non-sedating antihistamines first-line; add montelukast; omalizumab (anti-IgE) if persistent.
Autoimmunity — Mechanisms & Aetiology
The core defect = loss of self-tolerance (central thymic deletion + peripheral tolerance failing) → immune attack on self.
Contributors

INFECTIOUS DISEASE & IMMUNOLOGY__Viral I:
Overview — Viral Infections
The clinically important viral infections, grouped by family: the herpesviruses (sharing lifelong latency → reactivation) and the respiratory viruses (influenza, COVID-19).
The unifying herpesvirus principle: primary infection → lifelong latency → reactivation when immunity drops — which is why they dominate in immunosuppression (cross-ref T-cell deficiency).
Antiviral mechanisms: aciclovir → inhibits viral DNA polymerase; neuraminidase inhibitors → block viral release.
The Herpesvirus Family — shared biology
  • 8 human herpesviruses, all establishing latency: HSV-1, HSV-2, VZV (the alpha group — neurotropic, treated with aciclovir), EBV, CMV, HHV-6/7, HHV-8 (Kaposi's sarcoma)
  • Shared treatment principle: the "-ciclovirs" (aciclovir, valaciclovir, ganciclovir) inhibit viral DNA polymerase; resistance via mutation of viral thymidine kinase or DNA polymerase
  • Aciclovir SEs/toxicity: psychiatric (Cotard syndrome), toxicity → lethargy + myoclonus
HSV (Herpes Simplex Virus)
  • HSV-1 → cold sores around the mouth; HSV-2 → genital herpes (overlap exists — either can cause either)
  • Reactivation triggers: stress, infection, immunocompromise, UV light
Serious presentations: herpes simplex encephalitis (HSV-1, temporal lobe — the can't-miss; urgent IV aciclovir), neonatal herpes (HSV-2, peripartum), eczema herpeticum, herpetic whitlow.
Treatment: aciclovir (topical for mild cold sores; oral/IV for significant or systemic disease).
VZV (Varicella Zoster Virus)
📷 Image placeholder — Post-exposure prophylaxis — non-immune pregnant women and immunocompromised patients exposed to chickenpox need urgent antivirals/VZIG per current guidance; chickenpox in pregnancy risks congenital varicella syndrome
Primary = chickenpox
Fever + vesicular rash (lesions at different stages); most infectious 1–2 days before the rash appears.
Reactivation = shingles
Painful rash in a dermatomal distribution (doesn't cross the midline).
Complications: post-herpetic neuralgia, Ramsay Hunt syndrome (facial nerve → facial palsy + ear vesicles), ophthalmic zoster (V1 — Hutchinson's sign, sight-threatening); severe in pregnancy and immunocompromise.
Treatment: aciclovir / valaciclovir; cross-ref shingles vaccine (offered at 65; Shingrix, recombinant/non-live).
EBV (Epstein-Barr Virus)
  • Infectious mononucleosis ("kissing disease", glandular fever): fever, malaise, sore throat, lymphadenopathy, hepatosplenomegaly, transient macular rash
The amoxicillin trap: giving amoxicillin/ampicillin to someone with EBV → florid maculopapular rash (a classic SBA clue).
  • Investigations: raised lymphocytes (atypical lymphocytes), Monospot/heterophile antibody test (positive in the 2nd week)
  • Management: conservative (resolves in 2–4 weeks); avoid contact sport ~4–6 weeks (splenic rupture risk)
  • Malignancy associations: Burkitt's lymphoma, nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Hodgkin's lymphoma, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease
CMV (Cytomegalovirus)
📷 Image placeholder — CMV in transplant recipients — a leading opportunistic infection post solid-organ/stem-cell transplant, monitored by CMV viral load (PCR), managed with valganciclovir prophylaxis or pre-emptive therapy
  • Immunocompetent: typically a mononucleosis-like illness (but Monospot-negative — the discriminator from EBV); dormant in monocytes
  • Immunocompromised (the real importance): retinitis (HIV/AIDS), colitis, oesophagitis, pneumonitis, hepatitis
  • Congenital CMV: the commonest congenital infection → sensorineural deafness, microcephaly, growth restriction
Treatment: ganciclovir / valganciclovir.
Adenovirus — the CSP "ACE" trio
  • Normally self-limiting keratoconjunctivitis, respiratory tract infection, and gastroenteritis
  • In immunocompromise: encephalitis, pneumonitis, enterocolitis, hepatitis, haemorrhagic cystitis
Influenza
  • Presentation: abrupt fever, coryzal symptoms, lethargy, anorexia, arthralgia, headache, dry cough, sore throat (more systemic/abrupt than a common cold)
  • At-risk groups: elderly, pregnant, chronic disease, immunocompromised
  • Complications: pneumonia — primary viral or secondary bacterial (Staph aureus, pneumococcus)
  • Diagnosis: viral nasal/throat swab PCR
Management: most supportive; if at risk + within 48h: oral oseltamivir or inhaled zanamivir (neuraminidase inhibitors — block sialic acid cleavage → prevent viral release); annual vaccination for prevention.
COVID-19
  • SARS-CoV-2 — single-strand positive-sense RNA virus; incubation up to 14 days
  • Presentation: anosmia, cough, fever, myalgia, headache, fatigue; respiratory failure if severe
  • Diagnosis: RT-PCR of upper respiratory swab; CXR = bilateral lower-zone ground-glass infiltrates
Management: mild–moderate → supportive; hospitalised/severe → dexamethasone + remdesivir (nucleotide analogue) + CPAP/respiratory support, escalating to ventilation.
Long COVID: persistent fatigue, breathlessness, cognitive symptoms weeks–months after infection.

Bacteria Classification

Gram Positive (thick peptidoglycan, no outer lipid membrane)

  • Rods: Corynebacterium, Mycobacteria, Listeria, Bacillus, Nocardia

MRSA: Staph aureus resistant to beta-lactams (penicillins, cephalosporins, carbapenems) via altered penicillin-binding protein (PBP2a). Treatment options: doxycycline, clindamycin, vancomycin, teicoplanin, linezolid.
Antibiotic Classes — Mechanism & Key Side Effects
🔵
Penicillins (beta-lactams)
Inhibit cell wall synthesis (block transpeptidation). Amoxicillin, flucloxacillin, piperacillin. SEs: allergic reactions, cholestasis (co-amoxiclav — the classic cholestatic DILI; also amoxicillin), hypokalaemia/sodium load (piperacillin-tazobactam); flucloxacillin → delayed cholestatic hepatitis. Amoxicillin + EBV = rash.
🔵
Cephalosporins / Carbapenems
Inhibit cell wall synthesis (beta-lactams). Cefuroxime, ceftriaxone, meropenem. SEs: C. diff infection (especially cephalosporins — most common cause of C. diff). Penicillin allergy: ~1–2% cross-reactivity (side-chain dependent) with cephalosporins, ~1% with carbapenems.
🟣
Glycopeptides
Inhibit cell wall synthesis (non-beta-lactam mechanism — bind D-Ala-D-Ala). Vancomycin, teicoplanin. Uses: MRSA, C. diff (oral vancomycin for C. diff — not IV). SEs: nephrotoxicity, red man syndrome (vancomycin — slow infusion to prevent). Ototoxicity.
🟡
Aminoglycosides
Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome). Gentamicin, streptomycin. SEs: ototoxicity (irreversible — check levels after 3 doses), nephrotoxicity. Do NOT use in myasthenia gravis (blocks NMJ). Dose by ideal body weight in obese patients.
🟡
Tetracyclines
Inhibit protein synthesis (30S ribosome). Doxycycline. SEs: photosensitivity, teeth discolouration (avoid in children <8 and pregnancy). Used for atypicals, Rickettsia, Chlamydia, Lyme disease, brucellosis.
🟠
Macrolides
Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome — block translocation). Clarithromycin, erythromycin. SEs: QTc prolongation, P450 inhibitor (↑ statin levels → myopathy/rhabdomyolysis), cholestatic jaundice, tinnitus, GI upset. Do NOT use with statins.
🟠
Lincosamides
Inhibit protein synthesis (50S ribosome). Clindamycin. SEs: C. diff infection (highest risk). Used for anaerobic infections, dental abscesses, bone/joint infections.
🔴
Fluoroquinolones
Inhibit DNA gyrase (topoisomerase II) → oral, excellent bioavailability. Ciprofloxacin, levofloxacin. SEs: C. diff risk, tendonitis/Achilles rupture, lowers seizure threshold, dizziness, photosensitivity, prolongs QTc. Avoid in epilepsy, pregnancy.
🟢
Folate antagonists (trimethoprim, co-trimoxazole)
Inhibit folate synthesis (sequential blockade). Trimethoprim = first-line uncomplicated UTI; co-trimoxazole (+ sulfamethoxazole) = PCP treatment/prophylaxis. SEs: trimethoprim is a folate antagonist → teratogenic (1st trimester) + hyperkalaemia + raised creatinine; sulfonamides → Stevens-Johnson, haemolysis in G6PD.
⚫
Metronidazole
Bactericidal vs anaerobes + protozoa (C. diff, Giardia, bacterial vaginosis, abscesses) — causes DNA damage. SE: disulfiram-like reaction with alcohol (the classic exam point), peripheral neuropathy.
🟤
Nitrofurantoin
Concentrated in urine → uncomplicated UTI only. Avoid at term (neonatal haemolysis) and in significant renal impairment (needs renal function to concentrate in urine). Cross-ref UTI + drugs-in-pregnancy notes.
Penicillin allergy: ~1–2% cross-reactivity (side-chain dependent) with cephalosporins, ~1% with carbapenems. True anaphylaxis to penicillin → avoid ALL β-lactams; use a non-β-lactam.

Antibiotic Resistance Mechanisms
📷 Image placeholder — Four resistance mechanisms — enzymatic inactivation (β-lactamase/ESBL), altered target (PBP2a, gyrase, RNA pol, D-Ala-D-Lac), efflux pump and reduced porin permeability
🎯
Altered Target
Mutation in target site: RNA polymerase (rifampicin), DNA gyrase (ciprofloxacin), 30S ribosome (streptomycin). Altered PBP in MRSA.
🔄
Enzymatic Inactivation
Beta-lactamase destroys beta-lactam ring (penicillinase, ESBLs). Aminoglycoside-modifying enzymes. Co-amoxiclav = amoxicillin + clavulanate (beta-lactamase inhibitor).
💧
Efflux Pumps
Active transport pumps antibiotic out of cell. Affects: tetracyclines, quinolones, beta-lactams, macrolides. Common in Pseudomonas.
🔀
Alternative Target / Reduced Permeability
Using alternative metabolic pathway (vancomycin resistance: D-Ala-D-Lac). Reduced outer membrane porins (Pseudomonas). Biofilm formation.
Antifungals
  • All act on fungal cell wall/membrane synthesis (fungi have ergosterol, not cholesterol)
  • Azoles (ketoconazole, fluconazole, voriconazole): inhibit ergosterol synthesis (lanosterol 14α-demethylase). P450 inhibitors → many drug interactions. Fluconazole for Candida; voriconazole for Aspergillus.
  • Polyenes (amphotericin B, nystatin): bind ergosterol → pore formation → membrane leak → cell death. Amphotericin B: highly nephrotoxic, electrolyte imbalances. Reserve for life-threatening infections.
  • Echinocandins (micafungin, caspofungin): inhibit beta-glucan synthesis → cell wall formation. Good for invasive Candida/Aspergillus. Less toxic than amphotericin.

Protein synthesis: 30S inhibitors = aminoglycosides + tetracyclines (remember: "A-T = 30"). 50S inhibitors = macrolides + lincosamides + chloramphenicol + linezolid.
C. diff risk hierarchy: clindamycin > cephalosporins > fluoroquinolones > broad-spectrum penicillins. First-line treatment now oral vancomycin OR fidaxomicin (NICE — fidaxomicin increasingly first-line; metronidazole no longer first-line; oral not IV — must reach bowel lumen).
Atypicals (Legionella/Mycoplasma/Chlamydia) have no cell wall → β-lactams useless → use macrolides/tetracyclines/quinolones.
Bactericidal (β-lactams, vancomycin, aminoglycosides, quinolones, metronidazole) vs bacteriostatic (macrolides, tetracyclines, clindamycin, trimethoprim) — pick cidal in endocarditis/immunocompromise.
Penicillin allergy: cephalosporins ~1–2%, carbapenems <1% cross-reactivity; true anaphylaxis → avoid all β-lactams.
Metronidazole + alcohol = disulfiram-like reaction. Trimethoprim = folate antagonist (teratogenic 1st trimester, hyperkalaemia, ↑creatinine). Nitrofurantoin: avoid at term + in renal impairment.
Gentamicin: peak and trough levels needed. Ototoxicity is irreversible — stop if hearing changes. Check levels after 3 doses (or daily in CKD). Do not use in myasthenia gravis.
Fluconazole + warfarin: CYP450 inhibition → ↑ warfarin levels → bleeding risk. Always check P450 interactions with azoles.
ESBL-producing organisms (Klebsiella, E. coli): resistant to all penicillins and cephalosporins. Treatment = meropenem (carbapenem). Increasing CRE — use colistin as last resort.

Many traveller fevers are notifiable — malaria, typhoid/enteric fever, VHF, measles, brucellosis, typhus (cross-ref notifiable diseases).
VHF risk assessment — the critical "stop and isolate" step: fever + travel to a VHF area (e.g. Ebola, Lassa) within 21 days → isolate + urgent specialist/public-health involvement BEFORE routine bloods.
Pyrexia of Unknown Origin (PUO)

PUO = fever >38.3°C on ≥3 occasions over ≥3 weeks, not diagnosed after 1 week of investigation (hospital) or 3 outpatient visits.

Causes by Category
  • Infective (30–40%): TB, endocarditis, abscess, EBV, CMV, HIV, typhoid
  • Malignant (20–30%): HCC, RCC, lymphoma, leukaemia
  • Inflammatory (20%): SLE, RA, Still's disease, temporal arteritis
  • Drug-induced: antibiotics (esp. beta-lactams), NSAIDs, antihypertensives, antihistamines
  • Undiagnosed (10–15%)

  • History: travel, sexual contacts, animal exposure, occupation, medications
  • Blood cultures (×3, different sites) + thick/thin blood films
  • FBC, CRP, LFTs, U&E, LDH, ferritin
  • Serology: HIV, EBV, CMV, hepatitis, syphilis, Brucella, Leishmania
  • CXR, CT chest/abdomen/pelvis

Key Tropical Diseases

🦟
Malaria
Plasmodium falciparum = most common + severe. Anopheles mosquito. Fever + sweating + headache + vomiting + pallor + jaundice + hepatosplenomegaly. Inv: thick/thin blood films (×3). Severe malaria: IV artesunate (1st line) or IV quinine + doxycycline. Uncomplicated: artemether/lumefantrine. Vivax/ovale have dormant liver hypnozoites → relapse → add primaquine (check G6PD first); falciparum has no hypnozoite stage (no relapse).
🦟
Dengue Fever
Aedes mosquito. Tropical infection. Classic triad: fever + rash + bone pain ('breakbone fever'). Sx range from fever/rash to haemorrhagic fever/shock (DHF/DSS). Treatment: supportive (careful with NSAIDs in dengue — bleeding risk). No antivirals.
🦟
Chikungunya
Aedes mosquito. Inc 1–12 days. Defining feature: severe polyarthralgia (can persist months). Fever + rash. Treatment: supportive (NSAIDs, physiotherapy).
🐕
Rickettsia
African tick typhus. Non-specific: fever + headache + rash (petechial/maculopapular) + myalgia. Black eschar at bite site. Treatment: doxycycline (azithromycin if pregnant).
🌏
Enteric Fever (Typhoid/Paratyphoid)
Salmonella typhi/paratyphi. After SE Asia travel. Sx: fever, headache, constipation then diarrhoea, dry cough, rose spots on abdomen. Inv: blood cultures (positive in week 1). Treatment: ceftriaxone or azithromycin first-line for South/SE-Asian-acquired disease (widespread fluoroquinolone resistance / XDR strains); ciprofloxacin only if confirmed sensitive. Vaccine not 100% effective.
💧
Schistosomiasis
Tropical parasitic flukes from fresh water. Eosinophilia + swimmer's itch. Katayama fever (acute). Chronic: hepatic fibrosis, bladder cancer (squamous cell). Urine/stool microscopy shows eggs (if <2 months: serology). Treatment: praziquantel (repeat in 2 months — only kills adults).
💧
Leptospirosis (Weil's Disease)
Fresh water exposure. Biphasic illness: initial septicaemic phase (fever, headache, myalgia) then immune phase. Severe (Weil's): jaundice + conjunctival suffusion + renal failure + haemorrhage. Treatment: doxycycline/amoxicillin (mild) or IV penicillin (severe).
🐄
Brucellosis
High prevalence in farming/animal-human contact areas or eating unpasteurised food. Inc 5–30 days. Fever + weight loss + night sweats + lymphadenopathy. Important cause of PUO. Inv: blood cultures (gold standard) + serology. Treatment: doxycycline + rifampicin or gentamicin (6 weeks total).
🪱
Amoebic Liver Abscess
Entamoeba histolytica (faeco-oral). Single mass usually right lobe — 'anchovy sauce' contents. Fever + RUQ pain + hepatomegaly. Amoebic dysentery: profuse bloody diarrhoea. Inv: USS + serology (95% positive). Treatment: oral metronidazole + diloxanide furoate (luminal agent to clear gut).
🪡
Tetanus
Mostly developing world (no vaccine). RFs: wounds contaminated with soil, manure, rusty metals. Prodromal malaise + fever → trismus (lockjaw) + muscle spasms + abdo rigidity + dysphagia → respiratory failure + aspiration pneumonia. Dx: clinical. Tx: ITU admission + tetanus IG + wound debridement + supportive care.
🩸
Viral Haemorrhagic Fever (Ebola, Lassa, Marburg)
Fever + bleeding + organ failure after travel to West/Central Africa (incubation up to 21 days). The isolation imperative: isolate + urgent specialist/public-health involvement BEFORE routine bloods — don't delay. Notifiable. (Yellow fever is a related mosquito-borne VHF — vaccine-preventable.)
Infections Causing Chronic Disease
  • HPV (16, 18) → cervical + anal + oropharyngeal cancer; HPV (6, 11) → genital warts
  • EBV → nasopharyngeal carcinoma, Burkitt's lymphoma (Africa), Hodgkin's lymphoma
  • HTLV-1 → Adult T-cell leukaemia/lymphoma
  • H. pylori → gastric cancer + MALT lymphoma
  • Schistosomiasis → squamous cell carcinoma of bladder
  • Hepatitis B + C → hepatocellular carcinoma
⭐ Exam Pearls
Malaria: always suspect in any febrile returning traveller. Falciparum can be fatal within 24–48 hours. Do not wait for thick blood film — treat empirically if suspicious. Cerebral malaria, respiratory failure, hypoglycaemia = severe features.
Vivax/ovale relapse from liver hypnozoites → primaquine (check G6PD first); falciparum has no hypnozoite stage so does not relapse.
Geography: Sub-Saharan Africa → falciparum/HIV/schisto; S/SE Asia → typhoid/dengue/vivax; S America → dengue/yellow fever/lepto; Middle East → brucellosis/MERS.
VHF: fever + travel to West/Central Africa within 21 days → ISOLATE + notify before routine bloods; don't delay.
Dengue + NSAIDs: traditionally avoided due to bleeding risk in haemorrhagic dengue. Paracetamol is preferred analgesia in dengue.
Typhoid: rose spots on abdomen in week 2 + relative bradycardia (pulse-temperature dissociation). Blood cultures most sensitive in week 1; stool/urine cultures in weeks 2–3.
Schistosomiasis: eosinophilia + travel to Africa/Middle East/SE Asia + water exposure = schistosomiasis. Katayama fever at 4–8 weeks post-exposure.
Leptospirosis: distinctive features are conjunctival suffusion (red eyes without discharge) + jaundice + renal failure. Associated with water sports/occupational exposure.

Live vs Killed Vaccines
📷 Image placeholder — Live-attenuated (MMR, BCG, rotavirus, VZV, yellow fever, nasal flu) vs inactivated/subunit — dosing, IgA production, adjuvant need, and pregnancy/immunosuppression contraindications
Live Attenuated Vaccines
  • Examples: MMR, VZV (shingles), rotavirus (oral), yellow fever, BCG, nasal flu
  • Single dose often sufficient (produces strong cell-mediated immunity)
  • Produces IgG + IgA antibodies
  • May cause mild disease — DON'T give to immunocompromised or pregnant
  • No adjuvant needed
Killed/Inactivated/Subunit Vaccines
  • Examples: IPV, DTaP, hepatitis B, pneumococcal, HPV, injectable influenza, meningococcal
  • Multiple doses needed + booster
  • Produces IgG only (not IgA)
  • Safe in pregnancy + immunocompromise
  • Adjuvant required to boost immunogenicity
Vaccine Mechanisms
  • Diphtheria + Tetanus: toxoid adsorbed onto aluminium adjuvant (inactivated toxin → antibodies against toxin, not bacteria)
  • Pertussis: 5 purified protein components (acellular — replaced whole-cell due to SEs)
  • Meningococcus + Hib: capsular polysaccharide conjugated to carrier protein (T-cell dependent response → memory)
  • Pneumococcus (PCV13): conjugate containing polysaccharide from 13 common capsular types
  • Hepatitis B: recombinant viral surface antigen (HBsAg)
  • MMR: live attenuated strains — given from 12 months (maternal IgG would neutralise earlier)
  • Rotavirus: live attenuated, oral — leading cause of severe diarrhoea/hospitalisation in infants
⭐ Exam Pearls
MMR timing: given at 12 months not earlier because maternal IgG (transplacentally acquired) would neutralise the live vaccine if given before this. Maternal IgG wanes by ~6 months.
Live vaccines + immunocompromise: absolute contraindication. Live vaccines in immunocompromised patients (HIV CD4 <200, on biologics, post-stem cell transplant) → risk of vaccine-strain disease.
Conjugated vs unconjugated polysaccharide: conjugated (PCV, Hib, MenACWY) elicit T-cell–dependent response → memory formation. Unconjugated only T-independent → no memory → not effective in <2 years.
Pertussis in pregnancy: maternal vaccination at 16–32 weeks → antibodies passively transferred to neonate → protects newborn for first few weeks before own vaccines. Particularly important as pertussis most dangerous in <3 month infants.
HPV 16 + 18 cause 70% of cervical cancers; HPV 6 + 11 cause 90% of genital warts. Gardasil 9 (9-valent) now covers 90%+ of cervical cancer-causing strains.
